theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Resurrection of Christ
summary: The historical resurrection; firstfruits; vindication; ground of our justification and hope
readingInstruction: Read 1 Corinthians 15:1-28 and Matthew 28:1-10. Today is a doctrinal pause on the resurrection of Christ. Notice the evidence, the meaning, and the consequences of the empty tomb.
settingTheScene: The resurrection of Jesus is the central claim of Christianity. Without it, as Paul says, the faith collapses. The four Gospels each tell of the empty tomb, and Paul lists the appearances. Matthew’s account is brief and vivid: an earthquake, an angel, and two women who meet the risen Lord. Today we think about what the resurrection of Christ is, why it matters, and how we know.
observation: “He is not here, for he has risen, as he said” (Matthew 28:6).
“And they came up and took hold of his feet and worshiped him” (Matthew 28:9).
“That he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4).
“Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive” (1 Corinthians 15:6).
“And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” (1 Corinthians 15:17).
“But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).
“For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25).
“That God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).
doctrinalFocus:
The resurrection of Jesus is the historical event in which God raised the crucified Jesus from the dead on the third day, in a real, physical, glorified body, never to die again. It was not a resuscitation, like Lazarus, who died again. Jesus was raised to a new kind of life: the tomb was empty, and yet his body had new powers. He could pass through closed doors, but he ate fish and invited Thomas to touch his wounds.

The evidence is strong. The tomb was empty, and Jesus’ enemies never produced a body. The women, whose testimony was not prized in that culture, were the first witnesses. He appeared to individuals, to groups, to the Twelve, and to more than five hundred at once. The disciples were transformed from frightened deserters to bold witnesses, willing to die for what they had seen. Even Paul, the persecutor, and James, the skeptical brother of Jesus, were changed. The earliest church worshiped on Sunday, the day of the resurrection.

The meaning is vast. First, the resurrection vindicates Jesus: he is the Son of God (Romans 1:4). Second, it confirms that his death was accepted as payment for sin: “raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). Third, it defeats death: he is the firstfruits, guaranteeing our resurrection. Fourth, it inaugurates the new creation: the age to come has begun, even though it is not yet complete. Fifth, it establishes his reign: he is seated at the right hand of the Father, and he must reign until all enemies are subdued.

Christians affirm the bodily resurrection, and it is non-negotiable. Some modern theologians have spoken of a “spiritual” resurrection or a change in the disciples’ faith, but the New Testament insists on an empty tomb and a real, physical body. Paul says without the resurrection our faith is futile. But “in fact Christ has been raised.”
interpretation:
In Matthew 28, two women come to the tomb at dawn. There is a great earthquake as an angel rolls back the stone and sits on it. His appearance is like lightning. The guards shake and become like dead men. The angel says, “Do not be afraid, for I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come, see the place where he lay.” Then, “go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen from the dead.” The women leave with fear and great joy. Jesus meets them: “Greetings!” They take hold of his feet and worship him. They touch him, which shows he is not a ghost. And he says: “Do not be afraid; go and tell my brothers to go to Galilee, and there they will see me.” Notice that he calls his frightened disciples “my brothers,” even after they deserted him.

Paul in 1 Corinthians 15 argues from the evidence and then from the implications. Verses 12 to 19 form a chain: if the dead are not raised, Christ is not raised; if Christ is not raised, preaching is empty and faith is futile; we are still in our sins; those who died in Christ are lost; we are the most pitiable of people. But the next verse breaks the chain: “But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.”

In verses 20 to 28, Paul shows the cosmic scope. Death came through a man, and the resurrection of the dead also comes through a man. In Adam all die; in Christ all will be made alive. Each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power. “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” Christ’s present reign is the fulfillment of Psalm 110. He reigns now, and the victory over death is certain. At the end, the Son is subjected to the Father, in a loving order within the Trinity, so that God may be all in all.

The resurrection is not simply a doctrine to affirm but a reality to live in. Because Christ is risen, we have forgiveness, hope, and purpose. We can face death without despair.
connection: Psalm 16:8-11 predicts the Holy One not seeing corruption (see Acts 2:25-32). Isaiah 53:10-12 foresees the servant’s vindication. Hosea 6:2 mentions the third day. Matthew 12:38-40 is the sign of Jonah. Luke 24 and John 20 to 21 record other appearances. Acts 1:3, 2:32, and 10:40-41 speak of witnesses. Romans 1:4, 4:25, and 6:4-5 give the meaning. Philippians 3:10 speaks of knowing the power of his resurrection. 1 Peter 1:3-5 speaks of a living hope. Revelation 1:17-18 shows the risen Christ holding the keys of death.
application:
Read the account of the resurrection in one Gospel (Matthew 28, Mark 16, Luke 24, or John 20) and notice the details.

Share the hope of the resurrection with someone who is grieving or afraid of death.

On Sunday, remember that you gather on the day of the resurrection.
prayerPrompts: Praise Jesus that he has risen as he said.
Thank him for the hope the resurrection gives.
Tell him what you want to say to someone about it.
